title: Famine as Fiscal Policy: How the East India Company Taxed Bengal's Dead to Repay Parliament

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Post-Plassey, the Company converted the Bengal diwani into a fixed land-tax annuity, seizing the revenue stream of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa before any famine pressure existed.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Company tax collectors maintained the fixed revenue demand through 1769-1770 while grain prices soared, structurally prioritizing shareholder remittance over subsistence in the tax-yielding provinces.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Famine mortality — estimated at roughly a third of the affected population in contemporaneous Company and Indian sources — was reported slowly to London, where the Company's insolvency, not the dead, framed parliamentary debate.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Parliament answered with the 1773 Regulating and Tea Acts: a 1.4 million pound loan to the Company, its monopoly left intact, serviced by the very Bengal revenue the famine had gutted the population to collect.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The 1784 India Act subordinated the Company to a Board of Control, recasting insolvency and famine as an accountability problem solved by parliamentary oversight — no forfeiture, no shareholder liability, extraction machinery preserved.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Company inherited the joint-stock monopoly charter east of the Cape and, via Plassey, the Mughal revenue-farming apparatus of Bengal, fusing corporate trade privilege with sovereign tax power.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1773-1784 acts created the permanent template of state-bailed monopoly: parliamentary 'regulation' that socialized the Company's debts while privatizing its monopoly rents.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Bengal land tax serviced the parliamentary loan and Company dividends, recirculating colonial extraction upward to British creditors and shareholders at the direct cost of the taxed famine population.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: This bailout-monopoly template — cheap monopoly goods dumped to service debt, exemplified by the Tea Act — set the mechanism for the 1773 Boston Tea Party and the state-chartered extraction conduits that followed.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The 'wicked monopoly company' framing reduces the episode to a morality tale of Company greed, resolved once Parliament asserted control.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: It obscures the ledger: Parliament did not break the monopoly or penalize the shareholders — it lent the Company 1.4 million pounds repaid from Bengal revenue, deepening the extraction loop it purported to reform.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Contemporaneous Company and Indian sources record fixed tax demand sustained through the famine, mortality near a third of the affected provinces, and the 1773 loan and 1784 subordination — a documented chain from tax collection to parliamentary bailout to continued monopoly.
